findings.quote: Acinar cells make inactive enzyme precursors (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, lipase, amylase)
findings.explanation: Only the proteases (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, plus procarboxypeptidases, proelastase and prophospholipase A2) are secreted as inactive zymogens and activated in the duodenum (trypsinogen by enteropeptidase). Pancreatic amylase and lipase are secreted in active form (lipase works with colipase and bile salts). The next sentence, 'The enzymes are only activated in the duodenum', therefore also overstates, and it sits uneasily with the page's own clinical section, where a raised blood lipase or amylase marks pancreatitis precisely because these active enzymes leak into the blood.
findings.suggestedFix: Say that acinar cells make the digestive enzymes, that the protein-digesting ones (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen) are made as inactive precursors activated in the duodenum, and that amylase and lipase are secreted in active form.

findings.quote: the basal ganglia (caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus), which shape movement and are lost in Parkinson's disease
findings.explanation: The caudate, putamen and globus pallidus are not 'lost' in Parkinson's disease. What degenerates is the population of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra (pars compacta) that supplies the caudate and putamen, so basal ganglia circuits malfunction. Loss of caudate and putamen tissue is the pattern of Huntington's disease. As written the sentence teaches the wrong lesion.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: '...which shape movement; in Parkinson's disease the dopamine-producing cells of the substantia nigra that supply them degenerate.'

findings.quote: NHS: How the heart works
findings.explanation: The URL attached to this title (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/coronary-heart-disease/) is the NHS 'Coronary heart disease' condition page; the same URL is titled 'NHS: Coronary heart disease' on anatomy/coronary and conditions/coronary-artery-disease. It is not a page on how the heart works and cannot support the chamber, valve, supply and conduction anatomy on this page, so the heart page has no real NHS source for its anatomy.
findings.suggestedFix: Retitle as 'NHS: Coronary heart disease' if it is kept for the clinical-relevance paragraph, and rely on the BHF and NHLBI entries (or add a textbook such as OpenStax A&P 2e) for the structural anatomy.

findings.quote: 10 bronchopulmonary segments per lung, each with its own bronchus and artery
findings.explanation: The right lung has 10 segments, but the left lung is conventionally taught, and described by surgeons and radiologists, as having 8 (apical and posterior fused as the apicoposterior segment, anterior and medial basal fused as the anteromedial basal segment); some texts give 9 or 10 by counting the fused pairs separately, and some nomenclature lists give 10 per side. '10 per lung' as a key fact is therefore misleading for the left lung. Moderate confidence only because 10 per side does appear in some lists.
findings.suggestedFix: State '10 on the right and usually 8 on the left (some texts count 9 or 10)', or drop the number.

findings.quote: A surgeon can remove any segment or group of segments along these planes with little bleeding and no loss of function in the remainder.
findings.explanation: Overstates the safety of liver resection and reads as a promise. Segmental planes allow anatomical resection with preserved inflow and outflow to the remnant, but resection is limited by how much functioning liver is left (a future liver remnant of very roughly a quarter to a third of liver volume in a healthy liver, more in cirrhosis or after chemotherapy), and hepatectomy carries real risks of bleeding, bile leak and post-hepatectomy liver failure.
findings.suggestedFix: Soften to: 'Surgeons can remove one or more segments along these planes, which limits bleeding and preserves blood flow and drainage of the remaining liver, provided enough healthy liver is left.'

findings.quote: Red flags such as leg weakness, numbness in the saddle area or loss of bladder control point to cord or cauda equina compression and need an urgent MRI.
findings.explanation: Red-flag symptoms of cauda equina or cord compression are listed but the reader is not told what to do. In the UK these need same-day emergency assessment (the cited NHS back-pain page advises urgent help, 999 or A&E, for numbness around the genitals or buttocks and for loss of bladder or bowel control); the MRI is what the hospital then arranges. Anatomy pages carry no urgent-care callout (the template renders one only for symptom, condition and first-aid pages), so this sentence is the only place the signal appears.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the action: 'These need emergency assessment the same day (call 999 or go to A&E in the UK); an urgent MRI then confirms the cause.'

findings.quote: which is why a chronic blockage can be survived while a sudden one is not
findings.explanation: Categorical and untrue: most people survive an acute coronary occlusion (a heart attack), particularly with prompt treatment. A sudden blockage is less well tolerated because collaterals have had no time to develop, not unsurvivable. The wording could be read as saying a heart attack cannot be survived.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: '...which is why a gradual narrowing may cause few symptoms, whereas a sudden blockage often causes extensive muscle damage.'

findings.quote: filter the entire blood volume some sixty times a day
findings.explanation: Inconsistent with the page's own figure of about 180 L of filtrate a day: 180 L divided by roughly 5 L of blood is about 35-40 times a day. The familiar figure of about 60 times applies to the plasma volume (about 3 L), so the sentence conflates plasma with blood.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'filter a volume equal to the whole plasma about sixty times a day' or simply 'about 180 litres of filtrate a day'.

findings.quote: which is why men over 65 are offered a screening ultrasound
findings.explanation: The NHS AAA screening programme in England (the cited NHS page) invites men in the year they turn 65; men older than that are not invited but can ask for a scan. 'Over 65' misstates the offer. Other countries use different ages and risk criteria, so a UK-first page should name England.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: '...which is why men in England are invited for a screening ultrasound in the year they turn 65.'

findings.quote: Superior mesenteric artery to the caecum, ascending and most of the transverse colon; inferior mesenteric artery to the rest
findings.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the distal third of the transverse colon through to the upper rectum (superior rectal artery). The lower rectum and anal canal, which the page counts as part of the large intestine, are supplied by the middle rectal (internal iliac) and inferior rectal (internal pudendal) arteries. The body text lists only left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal arteries, and the venous section already says the lower rectum and anal canal drain to systemic veins, so the arterial summary is the odd one out.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: '...inferior mesenteric artery to the distal transverse, descending and sigmoid colon and upper rectum; the lower rectum and anal canal come from the internal iliac system.'

findings.quote: Most flexion and extension in the cervical and lumbar spine; rotation mainly thoracic
findings.explanation: The neck has the largest range of rotation in the spine, about half of it at the atlantoaxial joint (C1-C2), as the page's own Regions section says ('the axis (C2) provides the peg on which the head turns'). Lumbar rotation is minimal and thoracic rotation is the main rotation of the trunk. 'Rotation mainly thoracic' contradicts the body text.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: 'Flexion and extension mostly cervical and lumbar; rotation mainly at C1-C2 and in the thoracic spine, very little in the lumbar spine.'

findings.quote: Most back pain arises from these muscles, ligaments and facet joints rather than the discs.
findings.explanation: Stated as established fact. In most episodes no single structure can be identified (non-specific back pain, the category used by NICE and the cited NHS page), and discs, facet joints, sacroiliac joints and soft tissues may all contribute. The sentence also downplays disc-related pain, which the page itself describes as a cause of sciatica.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: 'Most back pain is non-specific: no single structure can be blamed, and muscles, ligaments, facet joints and discs may all contribute.'

findings.quote: Statins, aspirin and blood-pressure control slow the disease.
findings.explanation: Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug that lowers the risk of clot-related events in people who already have coronary disease; it does not slow plaque growth, and guidance generally does not recommend starting it for people without established cardiovascular disease, where bleeding risk offsets benefit. Grouped with statins and blood-pressure control, the sentence reads as general advice to take aspirin.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: 'Statins and blood-pressure control slow the disease; antiplatelet medicines such as aspirin reduce the risk of clots in people who already have it, when prescribed.'

findings.quote: causes tearing chest pain radiating to the back and is a surgical emergency
findings.explanation: Aortic dissection is a medical emergency needing an immediate 999 call and hospital care. Emergency surgery is the usual treatment when the ascending aorta is involved (Stanford type A), whereas uncomplicated type B dissection is usually managed with blood-pressure and heart-rate control, with intervention for complications. 'Surgical emergency' is imprecise, and the sentence gives the reader no action for the red-flag pain it describes.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: '...is a medical emergency: sudden severe tearing chest or back pain needs an immediate 999 call; surgery is the usual treatment when the ascending aorta is involved.'

findings.quote: the connection between the two systems forms haemorrhoids when pressure rises
findings.explanation: Haemorrhoids are the engorged or prolapsed anal vascular cushions and are not formed by the portal-systemic anastomosis. That connection at the anorectal junction dilates into rectal (anorectal) varices in portal hypertension, which are a separate entity. The sentence perpetuates an old textbook equation of haemorrhoids with portosystemic varices.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: '...the connection between the two systems can enlarge into rectal varices when portal pressure rises; haemorrhoids are separate vascular cushions in the anal canal that swell with straining.'

findings.quote: 15 to 20 lobes of branching tubulo-alveolar glands, each draining through a lactiferous duct; about 5 to 10 ducts open on the nipple and carry most of the milk
findings.explanation: The numbers cannot both hold as written: 15-20 lobes each draining through its own duct implies 15-20 nipple openings, while the same sentence gives 5-10. The 15-20 figure is the classical textbook count; dissection and ultrasound studies (for example Ramsay et al., J Anat 2005; Love and Barsky 2004) found about 5-10 duct openings (range roughly 4-18) and no discrete lactiferous sinuses. The body text ('Every lobe empties through a lactiferous duct' beside 'about 5 to 10 openings', and the ultrasound remark) repeats the tension, and none of the listed references evidences the ultrasound-based statements (the OpenStax chapter is a general A&P text that I would expect to follow the classical account).
findings.suggestedFix: Say that the gland drains through about 5-10 (range roughly 4-18) lactiferous ducts, each serving a branching ductal system, and that older texts quote 15-20 lobes; add the imaging study as a reference or soften the 'ultrasound has not confirmed' sentence.

findings.quote: whose combined surface, roughly the size of a tennis court
findings.explanation: A popular exaggeration. The alveolar gas-exchange surface is usually given as about 70 square metres at rest (up to roughly 100-140 square metres at full inflation); a tennis court is about 195 square metres (singles) to 261 square metres (doubles).
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with 'about 70 square metres' or drop the comparison.

findings.quote: breaks down worn-out red cells into bilirubin
findings.explanation: Old red cells are removed mainly by macrophages of the spleen (also bone marrow and, to a lesser extent, the liver's Kupffer cells), which convert haem to bilirubin. The liver's job is to take up, conjugate and excrete that bilirubin in bile. Attributing the breakdown to the liver blurs the pathway that the page's jaundice discussion relies on.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: 'processes the bilirubin released when worn-out red cells are broken down (mainly in the spleen), conjugating it for excretion in bile'.

findings.quote: the radial artery is joined under the microscope to a recipient vessel in the groin, usually the deep inferior epigastric artery or a branch of the femoral artery
findings.explanation: The page gives operative anatomy (flap pedicles, recipient vessels, which nerves are coapted, staging, complication pattern) that none of the five listed references covers: WPATH SOC8 (Surgery chapter) and the UCSF guideline give eligibility and general options, the NHS page is a condition overview, the WHO page a classification FAQ and the GOV.UK document a screening leaflet. I found the content consistent with standard descriptions of forearm and thigh flap phalloplasty and metoidioplasty and saw no factual error, but the 'source-verified' label cannot extend to these details with the references as listed.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a surgical-anatomy source (peer-reviewed phalloplasty and metoidioplasty technique reviews or a plastic-surgery/urology atlas) for the flap, pedicle, recipient-vessel and nerve-coaptation statements, or phrase them in general terms.

findings.quote: The neoclitoris survives on the dorsal neurovascular bundle, the paired dorsal arteries (branches of the internal pudendal artery), the deep dorsal vein and the dorsal nerves
findings.explanation: Same issue as the neophallus page: technique-level anatomy (neurovascular pedicle of the neoclitoris, plane and relations of the canal, lining, 'commonly about 10 to 13 cm' depth, complication pattern) is not covered by the listed references (WPATH SOC8, UCSF guideline, NHS condition page, WHO FAQ, GOV.UK screening leaflet). I found the content consistent with standard descriptions of penile-inversion vaginoplasty and saw no factual error, but nothing listed backs these specifics, and the depth figure in particular is unsourced.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a surgical-anatomy or outcomes source for the neurovascular bundle, relations and depth figures, or soften them to general terms.

notes: All 15 entities were read in full (fields, sections, structures, references). The cap of 20 findings was reached, so lower-value candidates were trimmed; they are listed below in case the maintainers want them. (1) Pattern, references: most anatomy pages cite only condition-level pages (NHS COPD, NHS CKD, NIDDK pancreatitis, NHS type 1 diabetes, NHS/BHF coronary heart disease, NHS AAA) that cannot support the structural detail on the page (segment and lobe counts, named arteries and nerve levels, dominance percentages, sizes). The anatomy looks like standard textbook content and I found it largely accurate, but it is not backed by the listed sources; consider adding one standard anatomy reference per page. (2) Pattern, signposting: the page template renders urgent-care callouts only for symptom, condition and first-aid pages (site/entity.js), so red-flag statements on anatomy pages carry no action wording: spine (cauda equina, reported), aorta (dissection pain, reported), brain (names the FAST test but never says to call 999), knee ('a hot swollen knee may be gout, pseudogout or infection' with no note that a possibly septic joint needs same-day assessment). (3) Gender-affirming pages (neophallus, neovagina): I checked flap pedicles and recipient vessels (radial artery/cephalic vein, ALT on the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery, DIEA/femoral/great saphenous), nerve coaptation (lateral and medial antebrachial and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves to ilioinguinal and dorsal clitoral nerves; pudendal S2-S4), the neoclitoral dorsal neurovascular bundle, canal relations (between prostate/membranous urethra and rectum, through levator ani), lymph drainage, and the stated limits (no erectile tissue and implant needed, slow and incomplete sensory recovery, non-lubricating keratinised lining without lactobacilli, lifelong dilation, retained prostate, no cervix, cervical and breast screening routes). I found no factual error. Wording is neutral and respectful (assigned sex at birth, trans men/women and non-binary people included, ICD-11 'conditions related to sexual health' correct). Minor points not reported: neophallus key fact says metoidioplasty is 'in one stage with no donor site' (urethral lengthening and scrotoplasty can add stages, and a buccal mucosa graft, a donor site, is commonly used); pedicled ALT 'no microsurgery is needed' holds for the vessels only (nerve coaptation is still microsurgical); neovagina key fact 'Regular dilation for life' is stricter than the body ('unless regular penetrative sex maintains depth'); the breasts page says trans women taking feminising hormones 'for several years' are eligible for screening, whereas I recall the GOV.UK/NHS guidance giving a specific threshold (about five years; low confidence, check against the cited document). Two different NHS URLs are used site-wide for the gender dysphoria page (/conditions/gender-dysphoria/ and /conditions/gender-dysphoria-and-incongruence/); I cannot check offline which one resolves. (4) Other trimmed minor candidates: lungs breathing rate 12-16/min (UK clinical normal range is 12-20); lungs 'no connection to their neighbours' for segments (collateral ventilation exists); stomach 'anti-inflammatory drugs' should read NSAIDs; liver 'everything absorbed from the gut passes through the liver first' ignores lymphatic absorption of dietary fat; brain key fact 'vertebral arteries joining at the circle of Willis' (they join as the basilar artery); aorta 'about 2.5-3 cm wide' is the ascending aorta (infrarenal aorta is about 2 cm and 3 cm is the aneurysm threshold); heart 'narrowing... causes heart attacks' and 'CPR works because the heart is squeezed against the spine' are simplifications; knee 'Strong quadriceps and hamstrings are the best protection for the ligaments' is absolute; knee intro 'most often replaced' joint may not hold in every jurisdiction (I am not sure it holds for the UK, where hip and knee replacement numbers are of a similar order). (5) Checked and consistent: coronary dominance 85/8/7 per cent agrees with the heart page ('most people'); left main stem 1-2 cm (coronary) versus 'a few centimetres' (heart) is compatible; renal, hepatic, gastric and pancreatic supply and nerve levels (T4 nipple, T6-T10 pancreas, T11-L2 ureter, S2-S4 pelvic splanchnics, T12 aortic hiatus, L4 bifurcation, L1-L2 cord end) are correct. Quotes in this file were machine-checked against content/anatomy.json.
